about: Franki's grammar points, read by Read & Listen's server (grammar.py, which gives each its finder) and bundled into the app (src/core/grammar.ts). docs/grammar.md has the fields and the rules. An explanation's paragraphs are separated by a blank line, and **double asterisks** mark words in the language.

points.name: Preterite
points.note: Finished past events: hablé, comió, fueron
points.explanation:
The preterite is for things that happened and finished at a definite point in the past: **ayer comí paella**, "I ate paella yesterday". It tells a story's events, one after another.

Regular endings: -ar verbs take **-é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron** (hablé, habló); -er and -ir verbs take **-í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron** (comí, vivió). For -ar and -ir verbs the nosotros form is the same as the present (**hablamos**), so only the context tells them apart.

Many common verbs have their own stem: **tuve** (tener), **hice** (hacer), **dije** (decir). Ser and ir share one set: **fui, fue, fueron**.

The imperfect sets the scene or says what used to happen; the preterite says what happened: **llovía cuando salí**, "it was raining when I left".

points.name: Imperfect
points.note: Ongoing or habitual past: hablaba, comía, era
points.explanation:
The imperfect describes the past as it was going on: what was happening, what things were like, and what used to happen: **de niño vivía en Madrid**, "as a child I lived in Madrid"; **hacía frío**, "it was cold".

Regular endings: -ar verbs take **-aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -abais, -aban** (hablaba); -er and -ir verbs take **-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían** (comía, vivía). Only three verbs are irregular: **era** (ser), **iba** (ir) and **veía** (ver).

The yo and él forms are the same (**yo hablaba, él hablaba**), so the subject often comes from the context.

The preterite says what happened; the imperfect sets the scene around it: **leía cuando sonó el teléfono**, "I was reading when the phone rang".

points.name: Present perfect
points.note: Has done: he hablado, ha comido
points.explanation:
The present perfect is **haber** in the present plus a past participle: **he hablado**, "I have spoken"; **ha comido**, "she has eaten". The forms of haber are **he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, han**.

It's for the past seen from now: something in a period that isn't over (**esta semana he trabajado mucho**, "I've worked a lot this week") or an experience up to now (**¿has estado en México?**, "have you been to Mexico?").

In most of Spain it's also used for things that happened earlier today, where Latin America mostly uses the preterite: **hoy he visto a Ana** or **hoy vi a Ana**, "I saw Ana today".

Participles end in **-ado** or **-ido**, with some irregulars: **hecho, dicho, visto, escrito, puesto, vuelto, abierto, roto**. Nothing comes between haber and the participle: **lo he visto**, "I've seen it".

points.name: Pluperfect
points.note: Had done: había hablado, habían comido
points.explanation:
The pluperfect is **haber** in the imperfect plus a past participle: **había hablado**, "I had spoken". The forms are **había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían**.

It puts one past event before another: **cuando llegué, ya se habían ido**, "when I arrived, they had already left".

It's common for reporting what someone said had happened: **me dijo que había perdido las llaves**, "she told me she had lost her keys".

The participle is the same as in the present perfect, irregulars included: **había hecho, había visto**.

points.name: Future
points.note: Will do: hablaré, tendrá, iremos
points.explanation:
The future adds endings to the whole infinitive: **-é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án**. **hablaré**, "I'll speak"; **comerás**, "you'll eat"; **vivirán**, "they'll live".

A few common verbs use a short stem with the same endings: **tendré** (tener), **haré** (hacer), **diré** (decir), **podré** (poder), **saldré** (salir), **vendré** (venir), **querré** (querer), **sabré** (saber), **pondré** (poner), **habrá** (haber).

In conversation, **ir a** plus an infinitive is more common for plans: **voy a llamar**, "I'm going to call".

The future also makes a guess about now: **¿dónde estará?**, "where can he be?"; **serán las tres**, "it must be about three".

points.name: Conditional
points.note: Would do: hablaría, tendría, iríamos
points.explanation:
The conditional says what would happen: **me gustaría ir**, "I'd like to go"; **yo no lo haría**, "I wouldn't do it".

It adds **-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían** to the whole infinitive (hablaría, comería). Verbs with a short future stem use it here too: **tendría, haría, diría, podría, saldría**.

With si (if), the si part takes the imperfect subjunctive: **si tuviera tiempo, iría**, "if I had time, I'd go". It's also the polite way to ask: **¿podría ayudarme?**, "could you help me?"

The endings are the imperfect's for -er verbs, but the conditional keeps the whole infinitive: **comería** is "would eat", **comía** "was eating".

points.name: Progressive
points.note: Be doing: estoy hablando, estaba comiendo
points.explanation:
**Estar** plus a gerund says something is in progress: **estoy hablando**, "I'm speaking"; **estaba comiendo**, "I was eating".

The gerund ends in **-ando** for -ar verbs and **-iendo** for -er and -ir verbs (hablando, comiendo, viviendo). After a vowel -iendo becomes **-yendo** (leyendo, oyendo), and some -ir verbs change their stem (**durmiendo, pidiendo, diciendo**).

Spanish uses it less than English: the simple present often does the job (**¿qué haces?** can mean "what are you doing?"). It isn't used for plans: **mañana salgo**, not estoy saliendo, for "I'm leaving tomorrow".

Object pronouns go before estar or join the end of the gerund: **lo estoy leyendo** or **estoy leyéndolo**.

points.name: Present subjunctive
points.note: quiero que vengas, ojalá llueva
points.explanation:
The subjunctive follows que after a wish, a feeling, a doubt or a request: **quiero que vengas**, "I want you to come"; **me alegra que estés aquí**, "I'm glad you're here". It also follows **ojalá** (I hope), **para que** (so that), and **cuando** about the future (**cuando llegues, llámame**, "when you get here, call me").

It's made from the yo form of the present without its -o, with the vowel swapped: -ar verbs take **-e, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en** (hable); -er and -ir verbs take **-a, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an** (coma, viva). So **tengo** gives **tenga**, and **hago** gives **haga**.

Irregular: **sea** (ser), **vaya** (ir), **esté** (estar), **dé** (dar), **sepa** (saber), **haya** (haber).

After saying or believing, the indicative is used, and the subjunctive only in the negative: **creo que viene**, but **no creo que venga**.

points.name: Imperfect subjunctive
points.note: si tuviera tiempo, quería que vinieras
points.explanation:
The imperfect subjunctive is the subjunctive in the past and in unreal conditions: **quería que vinieras**, "I wanted you to come"; **si tuviera tiempo, iría**, "if I had time, I'd go".

Take the ellos form of the preterite, drop **-ron**, and add **-ra, -ras, -ra, -ramos, -rais, -ran**: **hablaron** gives **hablara**, **tuvieron** gives **tuviera**, **fueron** gives **fuera**. The nosotros form has an accent: **habláramos**.

There's a second set of endings in **-se** (**hablase, tuviese**), more common in Spain and in writing. Both mean the same.

**Quisiera** is a polite "I would like": **quisiera un café**.

points.name: เคย (have ever)
points.note: Experience: เคยไป, have been
points.explanation:
**เคย** before a verb says something has happened at least once, as an experience: **เคยไปเชียงใหม่**, "I've been to Chiang Mai".

**ไม่เคย** means "never": **ไม่เคยกินทุเรียน**, "I've never eaten durian".

To ask, add ไหม or หรือเปล่า: **เคยไปญี่ปุ่นไหม**, "have you ever been to Japan?" The answer is **เคย** ("yes") or **ไม่เคย** ("no").

เคย can also mean "used to": **เคยอยู่ที่นี่**, "I used to live here".

points.name: กำลัง (in the middle of)
points.note: Ongoing: กำลังกิน, is eating
points.explanation:
**กำลัง** before a verb says the action is going on right now: **กำลังกินข้าว**, "I'm eating".

It's often paired with **อยู่** after the verb: **กำลังทำงานอยู่**, "I'm working (right now)". อยู่ alone can do the same job: **ทำงานอยู่**.

**กำลังจะ** means "about to": **กำลังจะไป**, "I'm about to go".

Thai verbs don't change, so without กำลัง the time comes from the context: **กินข้าว** can be "eat", "ate" or "am eating".

points.name: จะ (will)
points.note: Future or intention: จะไป, will go
points.explanation:
**จะ** before a verb marks the future or an intention: **พรุ่งนี้จะไปตลาด**, "I'll go to the market tomorrow".

Thai verbs don't change for time, so จะ is often left out when a time word already says it: **พรุ่งนี้ไปตลาด**.

The negative is **จะไม่**: **จะไม่ไป**, "I won't go".

With **กำลัง** in front it means "about to": **กำลังจะออก**, "about to leave".

points.name: แล้ว (already, now)
points.note: Done or changed: กินแล้ว, have eaten
points.explanation:
After a verb, **แล้ว** says something has happened or a change has taken place: **กินแล้ว**, "I've eaten (already)". At the end of a sentence it often means a new situation, "now": **ฝนตกแล้ว**, "it's raining now".

Between two actions it means "and then": **อาบน้ำแล้วไปนอน**, "shower and then go to bed".

**...หรือยัง** asks whether something has happened yet: **กินข้าวหรือยัง**, "have you eaten yet?" The answer is **กินแล้ว** ("yes, I have") or **ยัง** ("not yet").

points.name: ต้อง (must, have to)
points.note: Obligation: ต้องไป, have to go
points.explanation:
**ต้อง** before a verb means "must" or "have to": **ต้องไปทำงาน**, "I have to go to work".

**ไม่ต้อง** means "don't have to" or "no need": **ไม่ต้องจ่าย**, "you don't need to pay". It's a common polite refusal: **ไม่ต้องครับ**, "no need".

Don't confuse it with **ต้องการ**, "to want or need" something: **ต้องการน้ำ**, "I need water".

ต้อง can also be a confident guess, "must be": **ต้องเหนื่อยแน่ๆ**, "you must be tired".

points.name: กว่า (more than)
points.note: Comparing: แพงกว่า, more expensive
points.explanation:
**กว่า** after an adjective or verb makes a comparison: **แพงกว่า**, "more expensive"; **ร้อนกว่าเมื่อวาน**, "hotter than yesterday".

The thing compared with comes straight after กว่า, with no word for "than": **เขาสูงกว่าฉัน**, "he's taller than me".

**ดีกว่า** often means "better" or "it would be better to": **ไปพรุ่งนี้ดีกว่า**, "better to go tomorrow".

**มากกว่า** and **น้อยกว่า** are "more than" and "less than": **มากกว่าสิบคน**, "more than ten people".

points.name: ที่สุด (the most)
points.note: Superlative: ดีที่สุด, the best
points.explanation:
**ที่สุด** after an adjective or verb makes a superlative: **ดีที่สุด**, "the best"; **ใหญ่ที่สุด**, "the biggest".

The group it's compared within comes after **ใน**: **ร้านที่อร่อยที่สุดในซอย**, "the tastiest place on the street".

**มากที่สุด** means "the most" or "best of all": **ชอบอันนี้มากที่สุด**, "I like this one best".

In speech it's also used loosely for emphasis: **สวยที่สุดเลย**, "so beautiful".

points.name: ถ้า (if)
points.note: Conditions: ถ้าฝนตก, if it rains
points.explanation:
**ถ้า** starts a condition: **ถ้าฝนตก จะไม่ไป**, "if it rains, I won't go".

The result often starts with **ก็**: **ถ้าว่าง ก็มาได้**, "if you're free, you can come".

Thai doesn't change the verb for an unreal condition. A word like **คง** (probably) often marks the result instead: **ถ้ามีเงิน คงซื้อไปแล้ว**, "if I'd had the money, I'd probably have bought it".

**ถ้าอย่างนั้น** means "in that case", often shortened to **งั้น** in speech.

points.name: เพราะ (because)
points.note: Reasons: เพราะว่า, because
points.explanation:
**เพราะ** or **เพราะว่า** gives a reason: **ไม่ไปเพราะฝนตก**, "I'm not going because it's raining".

The reason can come first, with **ก็เลย** or **เลย** for "so" in the result: **ฝนตก ก็เลยไม่ไป**, "it rained, so I didn't go".

**ทำไม** asks "why", and the answer often starts with เพราะ: **ทำไมมาสาย**, "why are you late?" **เพราะรถติด**, "because of the traffic".

**เพราะฉะนั้น** means "so" or "therefore", at the start of a sentence.

points.name: ไหม, หรือเปล่า (yes or no questions)
points.note: ไปไหม, are you going?
points.explanation:
**ไหม** at the end turns a statement into a yes or no question: **ไปไหม**, "are you going?"; **เผ็ดไหม**, "is it spicy?" In speech it's often said and written **มั้ย**.

To answer, repeat the verb: **ไป** ("yes") or **ไม่ไป** ("no"). There's no single word for yes or no.

**หรือเปล่า** (often **รึเปล่า**) asks "or not?", and is the usual choice about something that has already happened: **เขาโทรมาหรือเปล่า**, "did he call?" The answer **เปล่า** means "no".

**หรือยัง** asks "yet?": **กินข้าวหรือยัง**, "have you eaten yet?"

points.name: Perfect
points.note: Has done: ich habe gesagt, sie ist gegangen
points.explanation:
The perfect is the usual past in speech: **haben** or **sein** in the present, plus a past participle at the end of the clause: **ich habe Kaffee getrunken**, "I drank coffee" or "I've drunk coffee". It covers both.

Most verbs take haben. Verbs of movement or of a change of state take sein (**ich bin nach Hause gegangen**, **sie ist eingeschlafen**), and so do **sein** and **bleiben** (**ich bin dort gewesen**, **wir sind geblieben**).

Regular participles are **ge-...-t** (**gemacht, gekauft**); many common verbs end in **-en** and change their vowel (**getrunken, gegangen, geschrieben**).

Separable verbs put ge- in the middle (**eingekauft**), and verbs in -ieren or with be-, ver- or er- have no ge- at all (**studiert, verstanden**).

points.name: Simple past
points.note: Did: ich war, er ging, wir machten
points.explanation:
The simple past is the past of written stories and the news: **es war einmal**, "once upon a time there was"; **er ging nach Hause**, "he went home".

In speech it's used mostly for **sein**, **haben** and the modal verbs: **ich war müde**, **wir hatten Zeit**, **ich musste arbeiten**. Most other verbs use the perfect in conversation.

Regular verbs add **-te**: **machte, kaufte, wir machten**. Strong verbs change their vowel instead: **ging, kam, sah, trank, schrieb**.

The ich and er forms are the same: **ich war, er war**.

points.name: Pluperfect
points.note: Had done: ich hatte gesagt, sie war gegangen
points.explanation:
The pluperfect is **hatte** or **war** plus a past participle: **ich hatte gegessen**, "I had eaten"; **sie war gegangen**, "she had gone". Verbs that take sein in the perfect take war here.

It puts one past event before another: **als ich ankam, war der Zug schon abgefahren**, "when I arrived, the train had already left".

It often follows **nachdem** (after): **nachdem wir gegessen hatten, gingen wir spazieren**, "after we had eaten, we went for a walk".

points.name: Future
points.note: Will do: ich werde gehen, es wird regnen
points.explanation:
The future is **werden** plus an infinitive at the end: **ich werde morgen arbeiten**, "I'll work tomorrow". The forms are **werde, wirst, wird, werden, werdet, werden**.

In everyday German the present often does the job when a time is given: **morgen fahre ich nach Berlin**, "I'm going to Berlin tomorrow".

werden with an infinitive also makes a guess about now: **er wird schon zu Hause sein**, "he'll be home by now".

On its own, werden means "to become": **es wird kalt**, "it's getting cold". With a participle instead of an infinitive it's the passive: **das wird gemacht**, "that's being done".

points.name: Subjunctive II
points.note: Would, could: ich würde gehen, wenn ich Zeit hätte
points.explanation:
Subjunctive II says what would be or could be: unreal conditions, wishes and polite requests. **Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich kommen**, "if I had time, I'd come".

Most verbs use **würde** plus an infinitive: **ich würde gehen**, "I'd go". A few common verbs have their own forms, used more than würde: **wäre** (sein), **hätte** (haben), **könnte, müsste, dürfte, möchte** and **wüsste**.

For polite requests: **könnten Sie mir helfen?**, "could you help me?"; **ich hätte gern einen Kaffee**, "I'd like a coffee".

The umlaut matters: **ich hatte** is "I had", **ich hätte** "I would have".

points.name: Passive
points.note: Is done: das Haus wird gebaut, er wurde gefragt
points.explanation:
The passive is **werden** plus a past participle at the end: **das Haus wird gebaut**, "the house is being built"; **er wurde gefragt**, "he was asked".

The past uses **wurde**; the perfect is **ist ... worden**, not geworden: **das Haus ist gebaut worden**.

The doer, when named, comes with **von**: **das Buch wurde von ihr geschrieben**, "the book was written by her".

**Sein** plus a participle describes the result rather than the action: **die Tür ist geschlossen**, "the door is closed", against **die Tür wird geschlossen**, "the door is being closed". Spoken German often uses **man** instead: **man sagt**, "people say".

points.name: Modal verbs
points.note: kann, muss, darf, soll, will, möchte + infinitive
points.explanation:
Modal verbs go with an infinitive at the end of the clause: **ich kann schwimmen**, "I can swim"; **wir müssen gehen**, "we have to go".

They are **können** (can), **müssen** (must, have to), **dürfen** (may, be allowed to), **sollen** (should, be supposed to), **wollen** (want to), **mögen** (like) and **möchte** (would like).

In the singular most change their vowel, and the ich and er forms are the same: **ich kann, er kann**; **ich will, er will**; **ich muss, er muss**.

**Nicht müssen** means "not have to", not "mustn't": **du musst nicht kommen**, "you don't have to come". For "mustn't", use **nicht dürfen**: **du darfst nicht rauchen**, "you mustn't smoke".

points.name: Verb last after weil, dass, obwohl
points.note: Subordinate clauses: weil ich müde bin, dass er kommt
points.explanation:
After **weil** (because), **dass** (that), **obwohl** (although) and similar words, the conjugated verb goes to the end of its clause: **Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich müde bin**, "I'm staying home because I'm tired".

With two verbs, the conjugated one comes last: **…, dass er kommen kann**; **…, weil ich es gesehen habe**.

When this clause comes first, the main clause starts with its verb: **Weil ich müde bin, bleibe ich zu Hause.**

**Denn** also means "because" but keeps normal word order: **Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin müde.**

points.name: Passé composé
points.note: Did, has done: j'ai parlé, elle est partie
points.explanation:
The passé composé is the usual past in speech: **avoir** or **être** in the present plus a past participle: **j'ai mangé**, "I ate" or "I've eaten"; **elle est partie**, "she left".

Most verbs take avoir. Être goes with about fifteen verbs of movement and change (**aller, venir, partir, arriver, rester, naître, mourir** and their relatives) and with every reflexive verb: **je me suis levé**, "I got up".

With être, the participle agrees with the subject: **elle est allée**, **ils sont partis**.

Regular participles end in **-é** (parlé), **-i** (fini) or **-u** (vendu); common irregulars are **fait, dit, pris, mis, vu, eu, été, pu, voulu**.

points.name: Imperfect
points.note: Was doing, used to: je parlais, il était
points.explanation:
The imparfait describes the past as it was going on: background, states and habits: **il faisait beau**, "the weather was nice"; **quand j'étais petit, je jouais au foot**, "when I was little, I used to play soccer".

Take the nous form of the present, drop **-ons**, and add **-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient**: **nous parlons** gives **je parlais**, **nous finissons** gives **je finissais**. Only **être** is irregular: **j'étais**.

The je, tu, il and ils forms all sound the same.

The passé composé says what happened; the imparfait sets the scene: **je lisais quand il est arrivé**, "I was reading when he arrived".

points.name: Future
points.note: Will do: je parlerai, il sera, nous irons
points.explanation:
The future adds **-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont** to the infinitive: **je parlerai**, "I'll speak"; **nous finirons**, "we'll finish". Verbs in -re drop their final e: **je prendrai**.

Common irregular stems: **ser-** (être), **aur-** (avoir), **ir-** (aller), **fer-** (faire), **pourr-** (pouvoir), **viendr-** (venir), **verr-** (voir), **voudr-** (vouloir), **devr-** (devoir).

In speech, **aller** plus an infinitive is more common for plans: **je vais partir**.

After **quand** about the future, French uses the future where English uses the present: **quand j'arriverai, je t'appellerai**, "when I arrive, I'll call you".

points.name: Near future
points.note: Going to: je vais partir, on va manger
points.explanation:
**Aller** in the present plus an infinitive says what's going to happen: **je vais partir**, "I'm going to leave"; **on va manger**, "we're going to eat". The forms are **vais, vas, va, allons, allez, vont**.

It's the everyday way to talk about plans and what's about to happen, more common in speech than the future tense.

Object pronouns go before the infinitive: **je vais le faire**, "I'm going to do it". The negative wraps aller: **je ne vais pas venir**.

In the imparfait it means "was about to": **j'allais partir**, "I was about to leave".

points.name: Conditional
points.note: Would do: je parlerais, il serait, nous pourrions
points.explanation:
The conditional says what would happen: **j'aimerais venir**, "I'd like to come"; **ce serait bien**, "that would be nice".

It uses the future's stem with the imparfait's endings, **-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient**: **je parlerais**, **il serait**, **nous pourrions**.

With **si** (if), the si part takes the imparfait: **si j'avais le temps, je viendrais**, "if I had time, I'd come". It's also the polite way to ask: **je voudrais un café**, "I'd like a coffee".

**Je parlerai** ("I'll speak") and **je parlerais** ("I'd speak") sound almost the same, so the context usually tells them apart.

points.name: Subjunctive
points.note: After que: il faut que je sois, qu'il fasse
points.explanation:
The subjunctive follows **que** after a need, a wish, a feeling or a doubt: **il faut que je parte**, "I have to leave"; **je veux que tu viennes**, "I want you to come". It also follows **pour que** (so that), **bien que** (although) and **avant que** (before).

For most verbs, take the ils form of the present, drop **-ent**, and add **-e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent**: **ils finissent** gives **que je finisse**. For regular -er verbs the singular looks like the present (**que je parle**), so only forms you can see are subjunctive are counted in your texts.

Irregular: **sois** (être), **aie** (avoir), **aille** (aller), **fasse** (faire), **puisse** (pouvoir), **sache** (savoir), **veuille** (vouloir).

After **penser** and **croire**, the indicative is used, and the subjunctive only in the negative: **je pense qu'il vient**, but **je ne pense pas qu'il vienne**.

points.name: Past tense
points.note: Did, was doing: он читал, она пошла
points.explanation:
The past tense is made from the infinitive: drop **-ть** and add **-л**, then an ending for gender and number: **он читал**, **она читала**, **оно читало**, **они читали**.

It agrees with the subject's gender, not its person: a woman says **я читала**, a man **я читал**. The plural is always **-ли**.

Imperfective verbs say what was going on or used to happen (**я читал книгу**, "I was reading a book"); perfective verbs say it was done (**я прочитал книгу**, "I read the book (to the end)").

Some are irregular: **шёл, шла** (идти), **мог** (мочь), **ел** (есть).

points.name: Future with буду
points.note: Will be doing: я буду читать, он будет работать
points.explanation:
**Буду** plus an imperfective infinitive makes the future of an action in progress or repeated: **я буду читать**, "I'll be reading" or "I'll read". The forms are **буду, будешь, будет, будем, будете, будут**.

Perfective verbs have no буду future: their present forms already mean the future, **я прочитаю**, "I'll read (it through)". So буду never goes with a perfective verb.

On its own, буду is the future of быть, "to be": **я буду дома**, "I'll be at home".

points.name: Conditional (бы)
points.note: Would: я бы пошёл, если бы знал
points.explanation:
**Бы** with a past tense verb says what would happen or would have happened: **я бы пошёл**, "I'd go" or "I'd have gone". There's no separate tense; the past form with бы covers both.

In a condition, both halves usually have бы, and **если бы** starts the if part: **если бы я знал, я бы сказал**, "if I'd known, I'd have said".

It's also used for wishes and gentle suggestions: **я бы хотел кофе**, "I'd like a coffee"; **ты бы отдохнул**, "you should rest".

Бы usually comes after the first word or the verb, and shortens to **б** after a vowel in speech.

points.name: Imperative
points.note: Commands: читай, скажите, идите
points.explanation:
The imperative gives commands and requests: **читай**, "read"; **скажите**, "tell (me)"; **идите**, "go".

It's made from the present stem: after a vowel add **-й** (**читать → читай**); after a consonant add **-и** (**говорить → говори**), or **-ь** when the stress stays on the stem (**встать → встань**).

Add **-те** for вы, to one person politely or to several: **читайте, говорите**.

Imperfective imperatives are for invitations and ongoing actions (**садитесь**, "do sit down"); perfective ones for a single action (**закройте дверь**, "close the door"). With **не**, use the imperfective: **не говори**, "don't say it".

points.name: Verbal adverbs
points.note: While or after doing: читая, прочитав, улыбаясь
points.explanation:
Verbal adverbs say what else the subject was doing: **читая, он улыбался**, "reading, he smiled"; **прочитав письмо, она ушла**, "having read the letter, she left".

Imperfective verbs give an action at the same time, with **-я** or **-а** on the present stem: **читая, говоря, улыбаясь**.

Perfective verbs give an action finished first, with **-в** or **-вшись** on the past stem: **прочитав, вернувшись**.

They never change for person or gender, and their subject must be the main verb's. They're more common in writing than in speech.

points.name: Comparatives
points.note: Than: быстрее, лучше, более интересный
points.explanation:
The short comparative ends in **-ее** (often **-ей** in speech): **быстрее**, "faster"; **интереснее**, "more interesting". It doesn't change for gender or number.

Some are irregular: **лучше** (better), **хуже** (worse), **больше** (bigger, more), **меньше** (smaller, less), **дороже** (more expensive), **дешевле** (cheaper), **проще** (simpler).

"Than" is **чем**, or the thing compared goes in the genitive: **он старше, чем я** or **он старше меня**, "he's older than me".

The long form puts **более** before the adjective, which then agrees: **более интересная книга**, "a more interesting book".

points.name: θα (will, would)
points.note: θα πάω, I'll go; θα ήθελα, I'd like
points.explanation:
**Θα** before a verb makes the future: **θα πάω**, "I'll go"; **θα γράφω**, "I'll be writing".

With the perfective stem it's one action (**θα γράψω**, "I'll write (it)"); with the present stem it's ongoing or repeated (**θα γράφω**, "I'll be writing" or "I'll write regularly").

With a past imperfective form, θα makes the conditional: **θα ήθελα**, "I'd like"; **θα πήγαινα**, "I'd go".

The negative comes before θα: **δεν θα έρθω**, "I won't come".

points.name: να (to, so that)
points.note: θέλω να πάω, πρέπει να φύγω
points.explanation:
**Να** plus a verb does the work of the English infinitive, which Greek doesn't have: **θέλω να πάω**, "I want to go"; **πρέπει να φύγω**, "I must leave".

The verb after να has its own subject: **θέλω να έρθεις**, "I want you to come".

Like θα, it takes the perfective stem for one action (**να γράψω**) and the present stem for an ongoing one (**να γράφω**).

On its own it makes a suggestion or a wish: **να πάμε;**, "shall we go?" The negative is **να μην**: **να μην αργήσεις**, "don't be late".

points.name: Past tense
points.note: Did, was doing: έγραψα, πήγαμε, ήταν
points.explanation:
Greek has two past tenses. The simple past says something happened and finished: **έγραψα**, "I wrote"; **πήγαμε**, "we went". The imperfect says it was going on or used to happen: **έγραφα**, "I was writing".

Both take the endings **-α, -ες, -ε, -αμε, -ατε, -αν**.

The stress goes three syllables from the end, so a short past form adds a stressed **ε-** at the front: **γράφω → έγραψα**. Longer verbs don't need it: **διαβάζω → διάβασα**.

Common irregulars: **ήμουν** (I was), **είχα** (I had), **πήγα** (I went), **ήρθα** (I came), **είδα** (I saw), **είπα** (I said).

points.name: Perfect
points.note: Have done: έχω γράψει, έχει πάει
points.explanation:
The perfect is **έχω** plus a fixed form ending in **-ει**, the same as the perfective future's third person without θα (θα γράψει): **έχω γράψει**, "I have written"; **έχει πάει**, "he has gone". The forms of έχω are **έχω, έχεις, έχει, έχουμε, έχετε, έχουν**.

The second part never changes: **έχουμε φάει**, "we've eaten".

Greek uses it less than English. For something that just happened, the simple past is common: **μόλις έφαγα**, "I've just eaten".

It's natural for experience up to now: **έχεις πάει στην Κρήτη;**, "have you been to Crete?"

points.name: Pluperfect
points.note: Had done: είχα γράψει, είχαν φύγει
points.explanation:
The pluperfect is **είχα** plus the same fixed form as the perfect: **είχα γράψει**, "I had written"; **είχαν φύγει**, "they had left". The forms are **είχα, είχες, είχε, είχαμε, είχατε, είχαν**.

It puts one past event before another: **όταν έφτασα, είχαν φύγει**, "when I arrived, they had left".

With θα it means "would have": **θα είχα έρθει**, "I would have come".

points.name: Past tense
points.note: Did: byłem, poszła, czytaliśmy
points.explanation:
The past tense adds **-ł-** to the infinitive's stem, then an ending for person and gender: **byłem** (I was, said by a man), **byłam** (by a woman), **był** (he was), **była** (she was), **było** (it was).

The plural has two forms: **-li** for a group with at least one man (**byli, czytaliśmy**), and **-ły** for the rest (**były, czytałyśmy**).

The person is in the ending, so the pronoun is usually left out: **czytałem książkę**, "I was reading a book".

Imperfective verbs say what was going on (**czytałem**), perfective ones that it was done (**przeczytałem**, "I read it through"). Some are irregular: **poszedł, poszła** (pójść), **jadł** (jeść), **mógł** (móc).

points.name: Future with będę
points.note: Will be doing: będę czytać, będzie padać
points.explanation:
**Będę** with an imperfective verb makes the future of an action in progress or repeated: **będę czytać**, "I'll be reading". The forms are **będę, będziesz, będzie, będziemy, będziecie, będą**.

After będę you can use the infinitive or the past form that agrees with the subject: **będę pracować** or **będę pracowała**. Both are correct.

Perfective verbs make their future without będę: their present forms already mean the future, **przeczytam**, "I'll read (it through)".

On its own, będę is the future of być, "to be": **będę w domu**, "I'll be at home".

points.name: Conditional (by)
points.note: Would: chciałbym, gdyby
points.explanation:
The conditional adds **-by-** and a person ending to the past form: **chciałbym**, "I'd like" (said by a man); **chciałabym** (by a woman); **zrobiłby**, "he would do".

In a condition, **gdyby** starts the if part, also with the past form: **gdybym miał czas, poszedłbym**, "if I had time, I'd go".

The by can move forward in the sentence: **ja bym chciał** means the same as **chciałbym**.

It's the polite way to ask: **czy mógłby pan mi pomóc?**, "could you help me, sir?"

points.name: Questions with czy
points.note: Yes or no questions: czy masz czas?
points.explanation:
**Czy** at the start turns a statement into a yes or no question: **czy masz czas?**, "do you have time?"; **czy to daleko?**, "is it far?"

The word order stays as in the statement. In speech czy is often dropped and the voice rises instead: **masz czas?**

Inside a sentence, czy means "whether": **nie wiem, czy przyjdzie**, "I don't know whether he'll come".

Between two choices it means "or": **kawa czy herbata?**, "coffee or tea?"

points.name: Want, must, can + infinitive
points.note: chcę iść, muszę pracować, mogę pomóc
points.explanation:
**Chcieć** (want), **musieć** (must, have to) and **móc** (can) go with an infinitive: **chcę iść**, "I want to go"; **muszę pracować**, "I have to work"; **mogę pomóc**, "I can help".

Their present forms: **chcę, chcesz, chce**; **muszę, musisz, musi**; **mogę, możesz, może**.

**Nie musieć** means "not have to": **nie musisz przychodzić**, "you don't have to come". For "mustn't", Polish uses **nie wolno**: **tu nie wolno palić**, "you can't smoke here".

**Umieć** is "can" for a skill: **umiem pływać**, "I can swim".

points.name: Past tense
points.note: Did: var, gikk, spiste, bodde
points.explanation:
The past tense says something happened at a time that's over: **i går spiste vi fisk**, "yesterday we ate fish".

Regular verbs add **-et**, **-te**, **-de** or **-dde**: **snakket, spiste, prøvde, bodde**. Many can take more than one (**kastet** or **kasta**).

Strong verbs change their vowel: **var** (være), **gikk** (gå), **kom** (komme), **fikk** (få), **sa** (si), **tok** (ta).

The verb is the same for every person: **jeg var, du var, de var**.

points.name: Present perfect
points.note: Has done: har vært, har spist
points.explanation:
The present perfect is **har** plus a past participle: **jeg har vært i Bergen**, "I've been to Bergen"; **har du spist?**, "have you eaten?"

It's for the past seen from now: experience up to now, and things that matter now. With a time that's over (**i går**, "yesterday"), use the past instead: **jeg spiste i går**.

Regular participles end in **-et**, **-t** or **-d**: **snakket, spist, prøvd, bodd**. Strong ones vary: **vært, gått, kommet, tatt**.

With verbs of movement, **er** is sometimes used instead of har: **han er reist**, "he has left".

points.name: Past perfect
points.note: Had done: hadde vært, hadde spist
points.explanation:
The past perfect is **hadde** plus a past participle: **jeg hadde spist**, "I had eaten".

It puts one past event before another: **da vi kom, hadde toget gått**, "when we arrived, the train had left".

It's also used for unreal conditions in the past: **hvis jeg hadde visst det, hadde jeg kommet**, "if I'd known, I'd have come".

points.name: Future
points.note: skal reise, kommer til å regne
points.explanation:
Norwegian has no future ending. It uses **skal**, **kommer til å** or the present with a time word.

**Skal** plus an infinitive is for plans and intentions: **jeg skal reise i morgen**, "I'm going to travel tomorrow".

**Kommer til å** plus an infinitive is for predictions, what will happen whatever anyone plans: **det kommer til å regne**, "it's going to rain".

**Vil** can also mean "will", but more often it means "want to": **jeg vil hjem**, "I want to go home".

points.name: Passive
points.note: Is done: blir solgt, selges
points.explanation:
Norwegian has two passives. **Bli** plus a participle is the usual one in speech: **huset blir solgt**, "the house is being sold"; **han ble spurt**, "he was asked".

Adding **-s** to the infinitive is the other, for general statements, instructions and writing: **huset selges**, "the house is for sale"; **det kan gjøres**, "it can be done". It's used mostly in the present and after modal verbs.

The doer, when named, comes with **av**: **boka ble skrevet av henne**, "the book was written by her".

points.name: Polite ます form
points.note: Polite verbs: 行きます, 食べました, 飲みません
points.explanation:
Adding **ます** to a verb's stem makes it polite, the way you talk to strangers, colleagues and shop staff: **行きます**, "I go" or "I'll go". Friends and family use the plain form instead (**行く**).

It has its own past and negative: **行きました** (went), **行きません** (don't go), **行きませんでした** (didn't go). **行きましょう** is "let's go".

The stem is the form before ます: **食べる** gives **食べます**, **飲む** gives **飲みます**, and the two irregular verbs give **します** (する) and **来ます** (来る).

points.name: Past tense
points.note: Finished events: 行った, 食べた, 高かった
points.explanation:
The past ends in **た** (or **だ** after some verbs): **食べた**, "ate"; **読んだ**, "read". The polite past is **ました**: **食べました**.

It's formed like the て form, with た in place of て: **行って** becomes **行った**, **書いて** becomes **書いた**, **飲んで** becomes **飲んだ**.

Adjectives take it too: **高い** becomes **高かった**, "was expensive". After a noun or a な adjective it's **だった** (plain) or **でした** (polite): **静かだった**, "it was quiet".

points.name: ている
points.note: Going on, or a state: 食べている, 住んでいる
points.explanation:
A verb's て form plus **いる** says something is going on right now: **ご飯を食べている**, "I'm eating". In speech it's often shortened to **てる**: **食べてる**.

With a verb of change it describes the state that the change left: **結婚している**, "is married"; **窓が開いている**, "the window is open". With **住む** it's where someone lives: **東京に住んでいる**.

The polite form is **ています**: **待っています**, "I'm waiting".

points.name: Want to (たい)
points.note: Wanting to do: 行きたい, 食べたくない
points.explanation:
**たい** on a verb's stem says what you want to do: **日本に行きたい**, "I want to go to Japan"; **何か飲みたい**, "I want something to drink".

It changes like an い adjective: **食べたくない** (don't want to eat), **見たかった** (wanted to see). Add **です** to be polite: **行きたいです**.

It's for your own wishes, or a question to the person you're talking to. For someone else, Japanese says **行きたがっている** or **行きたいそうです** instead.

points.name: てください
points.note: Polite requests: 待ってください, 見てください
points.explanation:
A verb's て form plus **ください** asks someone politely to do something: **ちょっと待ってください**, "please wait a moment"; **ここに名前を書いてください**, "please write your name here".

The negative asks someone not to: **ないでください**: **触らないでください**, "please don't touch".

Among friends it's just the て form: **待って**, "wait". **てくださいませんか** is more polite still.

points.name: Let's (volitional)
points.note: Let's, I'll: 行こう, 食べよう, 行きましょう
points.explanation:
The volitional is "let's" or "I'll": **行こう**, "let's go"; **食べよう**, "let's eat". The polite form is **ましょう**: **行きましょう**.

Group 1 verbs change their last sound to **o** and add **う** (**会う** to **会おう**, **書く** to **書こう**); group 2 verbs take **よう** (**見る** to **見よう**). する and 来る give **しよう** and **来よう**.

With **と思う** it's a plan: **明日行こうと思う**, "I think I'll go tomorrow". **ましょうか** offers help: **持ちましょうか**, "shall I carry it?"

points.name: Conditionals (たら, ば)
points.note: If, when: 行ったら, 雨だったら, 行けば
points.explanation:
**たら** is the everyday "if" or "when", made like the past with ら: **雨が降ったら**, "if it rains"; **家に着いたら電話して**, "call me when you get home". After a noun it's **だったら**.

**ば** is a little more about the condition itself, often with advice or what follows naturally: **早く行けば間に合う**, "if you go early you'll make it". Verbs change their last sound to **e** and add ば: **行く** to **行けば**; い adjectives take **ければ**: **安ければ**.

When both work, たら is the safer choice in conversation.

points.name: Causative
points.note: Make or let someone do: 食べさせる, 行かせる
points.explanation:
The causative says someone makes or lets another person do something: **子供に野菜を食べさせる**, "make the children eat vegetables". The person made to act takes **に** (or **を** with a verb of motion).

Group 1 verbs change their last sound to **a** and add **せる** (**行く** to **行かせる**); group 2 verbs add **させる** (**食べる** to **食べさせる**); する becomes **させる** and 来る **来させる**.

With **てください** it asks permission: **私に払わせてください**, "please let me pay".

points.name: てしまう
points.note: Done completely, or by mistake: 忘れてしまった, 食べちゃった
points.explanation:
A verb's て form plus **しまう** says something is done completely, or happened when it shouldn't have: **宿題を全部やってしまった**, "I finished all the homework"; **財布を忘れてしまった**, "I (stupidly) forgot my wallet".

In speech it shrinks to **ちゃう** (or **じゃう** after で): **忘れちゃった**, **読んじゃった**.

Which meaning it has comes from the situation: finishing a task, or regret about what happened.

points.name: Respectful and humble verbs
points.note: Keigo: いらっしゃる, おっしゃる, 申す, いただく
points.explanation:
Keigo replaces everyday verbs with special ones. Respectful verbs raise the other person: **いらっしゃる** (to be, come or go), **おっしゃる** (to say), **召し上がる** (to eat or drink), **なさる** (to do).

Humble verbs lower yourself: **申す** (to say; **田中と申します**, "my name is Tanaka"), **参る** (to go or come), **いただく** (to receive or eat), **おる** (to be), **致す** (to do).

**ございます** is a very polite **あります**. You hear keigo from shop staff, at work and in formal speech, and it's usually in the ます form.
